Exercises

Problems to check your understanding of this chapter. The solutions are folded away — try them yourself first.

Easy

1Easy

With p1=2p_1 = 2p1​=2, p2=1p_2 = 1p2​=1, w=60w = 60w=60, find the two intercepts and the slope of the budget line.

Bp,w={x≥0:p1x1+p2x2≤w}B_{p,w} = \{x \ge 0 : p_1 x_1 + p_2 x_2 \le w\}Bp,w​={x≥0:p1​x1​+p2​x2​≤w}
  • The Budget Set
Show solution
  1. The x1x_1x1​-intercept is w/p1=60/2=30w/p_1 = 60/2 = 30w/p1​=60/2=30 and the x2x_2x2​-intercept is w/p2=60/1=60w/p_2 = 60/1 = 60w/p2​=60/1=60.
  2. The slope is −p1/p2=−2-p_1/p_2 = -2−p1​/p2​=−2 — the opportunity cost of one unit of good 1 is two units of good 2.

Medium

2Medium

At p=(1,1)p = (1, 1)p=(1,1), w=60w = 60w=60 the bundle (30,30)(30, 30)(30,30) lies on the budget line. When p1p_1p1​ rises to 222, is this bundle still affordable? Describe the geometric change of the budget line as well.

  • The Budget Set
Show solution
  1. The original intercepts were (60,60)(60, 60)(60,60). At p1=2p_1 = 2p1​=2 only the x1x_1x1​-intercept shrinks to 303030; the budget line rotates inward around the x2x_2x2​-intercept.
  2. The bundle (30,30)(30, 30)(30,30) now costs 2⋅30+30=90>602 \cdot 30 + 30 = 90 > 602⋅30+30=90>60, so it is no longer affordable. Bundles heavy in the now-expensive good are hit hardest — the geometry of the rotation made visible.
3Medium

With u(x1,x2)=x11/4x23/4u(x_1, x_2) = x_1^{1/4} x_2^{3/4}u(x1​,x2​)=x11/4​x23/4​, p1=2p_1 = 2p1​=2, p2=1p_2 = 1p2​=1, w=80w = 80w=80, find x1(p,w)x_1(p, w)x1​(p,w) and verify that doubling all prices and wealth leaves demand unchanged.

x1(p,w)=awp1x_1(p, w) = \frac{aw}{p_1}x1​(p,w)=p1​aw​
  • Walrasian Demand and the Demand Curve
Show solution
  1. With a=1/4a = 1/4a=1/4, x1=0.25⋅802=10x_1 = \frac{0.25 \cdot 80}{2} = 10x1​=20.25⋅80​=10.
  2. Doubling prices and wealth gives x1(2p,2w)=0.25⋅1604=10x_1(2p, 2w) = \frac{0.25 \cdot 160}{4} = 10x1​(2p,2w)=40.25⋅160​=10 — the factor of 2 cancels between numerator and denominator. The point on the demand curve does not move.

Hard

4Hard

For λ>0\lambda > 0λ>0, prove that B(λp,λw)=B(p,w)B(\lambda p, \lambda w) = B(p, w)B(λp,λw)=B(p,w), and deduce directly from the definition of the UMP that Walrasian demand x(p,w)x(p, w)x(p,w) is homogeneous of degree zero.

B(p,w)={x≥0:p⋅x≤w}B(p, w) = \{x \ge 0 : p \cdot x \le w\}B(p,w)={x≥0:p⋅x≤w}
x(p,w)=arg⁡max⁡x∈B(p,w)u(x)x(p, w) = \arg\max_{x \in B(p, w)} u(x)x(p,w)=argx∈B(p,w)max​u(x)
  • The Budget Set
  • Walrasian Demand and the Demand Curve
Show solution
  1. x∈B(λp,λw)x \in B(\lambda p, \lambda w)x∈B(λp,λw) means (λp)⋅x≤λw(\lambda p) \cdot x \le \lambda w(λp)⋅x≤λw. Since λ>0\lambda > 0λ>0, dividing by λ\lambdaλ gives p⋅x≤wp \cdot x \le wp⋅x≤w, i.e. x∈B(p,w)x \in B(p, w)x∈B(p,w). The converse is identical, so the two sets are equal.
  2. The UMP maximizes utility over the budget set, so equal sets give equal maximizers: x(λp,λw)=arg⁡max⁡B(λp,λw)u=arg⁡max⁡B(p,w)u=x(p,w)x(\lambda p, \lambda w) = \arg\max_{B(\lambda p, \lambda w)} u = \arg\max_{B(p, w)} u = x(p, w)x(λp,λw)=argmaxB(λp,λw)​u=argmaxB(p,w)​u=x(p,w).
    x(λp,λw)=x(p,w)∀λ>0x(\lambda p, \lambda w) = x(p, w) \quad \forall \lambda > 0x(λp,λw)=x(p,w)∀λ>0
  3. Scaling prices and wealth together leaves the budget set itself unchanged, so the choice cannot change either — the geometric reason behind the degree-zero homogeneity of demand.
